newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Casualty toll climbs in Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: Casualty toll climbs in Afghanistan.

text.p: At least 6,800 people have been wounded in fighting in Afghanistan over the last three months, the International Committee of the Red Cross said on Thursday.

"In May, June and July more than 6,800 war wounded -- civilian and military, on both sides of the front line -- received assistance from the Red Cross, 70 percent of them as a result of the fighting north of Kabul," said Thomas Gurtner, acting head of the ICRC in Afghanistan.
He said the number did not include those who had died in the conflict.
"It is impossible to estimate the number of deaths," he said.

Fighting flared in May when forces of the purist Islamic Taleban made an abortive attempt to take the north of the country with the assistance of an opposition commander who had defected to their side.
The mission went disastrously wrong when the commander, General Abdul Malik, turned on the Taleban and drove them from the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif with heavy losses.

The main theatre of war then switched to the Shomali valley, which runs north from Kabul into the foothills of the Hindu Kush mountains. Three weeks ago the opposition managed to advance south down the valley to within 12 miles (20 km) of Kabul.
Since then there has been little significant change in the front line, but there have been sporadic attacks and fierce exchanges of artillery and rocket fire on a daily basis.
The ICRC statistics do not distinguish between civilian and military casualties and Gurtner says that the real number of wounded is probably higher.
"These are just the people whom we have treated or otherwise provided assistance to," he said.
Witnesses who on Tuesday visited a hospital in the opposition-controlled town of Charikar, 40 miles (64 km) north of Kabul, described seeing children who had been injured in air attacks.
Among them was six-year-old Nabila, who suffered fearful head and face injuries from shrapnel from a Taleban air raid near her frontline village.
Much of the civilian population of the fertile Shomali valley had been moved from the area by the Taleban before the opposition offensive to prevent guerrilla attacks on their forces.

Most of the few remaining residents have now left the area. The United Nations estimates that Kabul's population has been swollen by as many as 200,000 people displaced from the Shomali since the beginning of the year.

"The majority of the displaced people have lodged with friends and relatives, adding to the problems facing the city's impoverished inhabitants. A few hundred are living in public buildings, where they receive periodic assistance from the ICRC," a recent U.N. report said.
